spreads.title: How computers get faster
spreads.concept: A tiny course written by hand to show every PopBook scene block. Each spread uses a different block; open them one by one and touch everything.
plan: From source code to machine code (flow)
spreads.fig: Fig. 0 — Four objects scientists simulate. Touch each one.

items.label: Chemistry
items.tip: Simulating how atoms move needs billions of small steps.

items.label: Genomics
items.tip: Comparing genomes means matching billions of letters.

items.label: Engineering
items.tip: Stress in a part is computed on a mesh of small elements.

items.label: Pharmacy
items.tip: Millions of candidate molecules are scored by computer.

spreads.title: Amdahl's law: the serial part wins
spreads.concept: If a fraction p of a program can run in parallel, n processors speed it up by at most 1/((1−p)+p/n). The serial part caps the gain, however many cores you add.
vocab: time on 1 processor ÷ time on n processors.
the fraction p that can be split.
1 − p, must run on one core.

quiz.q: With p = 0.9, what is the best speed-up you can ever reach?

spreads.why: When n grows, p/n shrinks to zero and only the serial 10 % remains: S → 1/0.1 = 10. Drag the slider to p = 0.99 and the ceiling rises to 100.
spreads.fig: Fig. 1 — Speed-up versus processors. Move the slider, then touch the curve.

spreads.title: From source code to machine code
spreads.concept: A compiler works like an assembly line. Each stage takes the output of the previous one and hands a more precise form to the next.

formula.label: PIPELINE
formula.eq: text → tokens → tree → optimized tree → machine code
formula.note: Real compilers have more stages; these five are the classic ones.

vocab: a word of the language: name, number, symbol.
the program's grammar as a tree.
rewrites the tree to run faster.
turns the tree into CPU instructions.

quiz.q: Which stage first notices a missing parenthesis?

spreads.why: The lexer only cuts the text into tokens; a lone parenthesis is still a valid token. The parser checks the grammar and fails when the tree cannot be built.
spreads.fig: Fig. 2 — Press Run on the left page, or touch each stage.

steps.label: Source
steps.tip: The program as plain text written by a person.

steps.label: Lexer
steps.tip: Cuts the text into tokens: names, numbers, symbols.

steps.label: Parser
steps.tip: Checks the grammar and builds a syntax tree.

steps.label: Optimizer
steps.tip: Removes useless work and simplifies the tree.

steps.label: Code gen
steps.tip: Emits machine instructions for the target CPU.

spreads.title: A computer is a stack of layers
spreads.concept: Each layer hides the details of the one below. An app never talks to transistors: it asks the runtime, which asks the OS, which drives the hardware.

formula.label: IDEA
formula.eq: each layer = a simpler interface over the one below

quiz.q: A game wants to read a file. Who actually talks to the disk?

spreads.why: The game calls a library function, the runtime turns it into a system call, and only the operating system drives the disk controller.
spreads.fig: Fig. 3 — Four layers, bottom to top. Touch each floor.

levels.title: HARDWARE
levels.tip: The physical machine: it only understands instructions and addresses.

levels.title: OS
levels.tip: Shares CPU time, memory and devices between programs.

levels.title: RUNTIME
levels.tip: Memory allocation, threads, file APIs for one language.

levels.title: APP
levels.tip: Your program: it only sees the layer just below.

spreads.title: Queues fill up suddenly
spreads.concept: A server handles μ = 10 requests per second. While requests arrive slower than that the queue stays short; near the limit it fills up fast and overflows.

formula.label: LOAD
formula.note: Standard queueing result (M/M/1): mean wait = 1/(μ − λ), not from a slide.

vocab: utilisation: share of time the server is busy.

quiz.q: Going from 80 % to 95 % load, what happens to the waiting time?

spreads.why: Wait = 1/(μ − λ): at λ = 8 it is 0.5 s, at λ = 9.5 it is 2 s, four times longer. Push the slider toward 10 and watch the tank.
spreads.fig: Fig. 4 — A tank as a queue. Move the arrival rate slider.

threshold.label: overload
threshold.tip: When λ ≥ μ the queue grows without limit.

messages.text: Overload: requests arrive faster than they are served.
Almost full: tiny changes in load make huge waits.
Plenty of room: requests are served almost at once.

spreads.title: Current through a resistor
spreads.concept: Push a voltage across a resistor and a current flows. Double the voltage and the current doubles; double the resistance and it halves.

formula.label: OHM
formula.note: Standard physics, added for the demo.

vocab: how hard the part resists, in ohms.
breaks the circuit when I is too large.

quiz.q: With R = 10 Ω, which voltage gives a current of 1 A?

spreads.why: I = V/R so V = I·R = 1 × 10 = 10 V. With the 20 Ω resistor you need 20 V for the same current: try the toggle.
spreads.fig: Fig. 5 — A current dial. Slide the voltage, switch the resistor.

threshold.label: fuse 2 A
threshold.tip: With 10 Ω, 20 V means 2 A: the fuse blows.

spreads.title: One core, four programs
spreads.concept: A single core runs one program at a time. The scheduler gives each a short slice in turn; with small slices everything seems to run at once.

formula.label: ROUND ROBIN
formula.eq: each task runs for one quantum, then goes to the back of the queue

vocab: saving one task, loading the next.
two hardware threads share one core.

quiz.q: What does a smaller quantum change for the user?

spreads.why: Each program waits less between turns, so all of them respond smoothly; total work is the same and switching even costs a little time.
spreads.fig: Fig. 6 — Touch the core to start, then change the quantum.

spreads.title: CPU against GPU
spreads.concept: A GPU has thousands of simple cores. On work made of many identical small tasks it leaves the CPU far behind; on a single long chain of steps it cannot help.

formula.label: RULE
formula.eq: many independent tasks → GPU · one long chain → CPU
formula.note: Times are illustrative orders of magnitude for this demo.

vocab: few powerful cores, good at branching code.
thousands of simple cores in lock-step.
small function run by every GPU core.

quiz.q: Which job gains least from a GPU?

spreads.why: Each step of the loop needs the previous one, so the work cannot be spread. Photos and matrix cells are independent and run side by side.
spreads.fig: Fig. 7 — CPU (violet) vs GPU (blue). Touch each job to start the clock.

items.label: Loop
items.tip: A step-by-step simulation: each step needs the last.

spreads.title: Typical laptop memory
spreads.concept: Laptop memory has grown steadily. On a linear scale the last bars dominate; switch to log to see the growth rate.

formula.label: TREND
formula.note: Rounded typical values, for the demo.

vocab: fast working memory, emptied at power-off.
equal steps add the same amount.

quiz.q: On a linear scale, how does the 2005 bar look next to 2025?

spreads.why: 0.5 GB is 1/64 of 32 GB, so its bar is barely visible. A log scale gives every doubling the same height.
spreads.fig: Fig. 8 — Press grow, then switch the scale.

spreads.title: Simple shapes, one per idea
spreads.concept: The showcase block can also show plain shapes when an idea has no obvious object. Here a globe cycles through steps and two shapes spin when touched.

formula.label: STEPS

one state of an item; touch to cycle.

quiz.q: Halving the grid spacing on a map multiplies the number of points by…

spreads.why: Both directions get twice as many points: 2 × 2 = 4. Touch the globe twice and watch the grid refine.
spreads.fig: Fig. 9 — A globe with steps, a pyramid and a cylinder. Touch all three.

items.label: Weather

items.label: Cylinder

spreads.title: Many machines, one job
spreads.concept: A cluster links ordinary computers through a fast switch. The job is split, pieces travel over the network, and results come back to be combined.

formula.label: COST
formula.note: Simplified model for the demo: more nodes also means more messages.

vocab: box that forwards packets between nodes.
time for one message to arrive.

quiz.q: Why does adding nodes eventually stop helping?
opts: nodes slow each other down on purpose

spreads.why: Each extra node shrinks compute/n but adds messages. Past some point the network time dominates and the job gets no faster.
spreads.fig: Fig. 10 — Five nodes around a switch. Touch any machine to send packets.

spreads.title: A custom scene: the pendulum
spreads.concept: When no block fits, an agent can write a scene module with the kit API. This pendulum swings with the period given by its length.

formula.label: PERIOD
formula.note: Small-angle approximation, standard physics added for the demo.

vocab: from the pivot to the weight.

quiz.q: Make the string 4 times longer. The period…

spreads.why: T grows with the square root of L: √4 = 2, so the swing takes twice as long. The mass does not appear in the formula at all.
spreads.fig: Fig. 11 — Touch the weight to start it, then change the length.
